My (informal) understanding is that under pressure from the vehicle's weight, the tip of the studs protrude slightly, but enough to present a hard surface pressing into and therefore against the hard ice. On deceleration (braking), the ice may give, and break away, but as the tire rotates, another set of studs impinges on a new area of ice. And, of course. the tire tread itself still presents friction and some similar impingement by the exposed rubber edge.

So ... studs add another dimension of resistance on stopping.

Now, this isn't an argument that you NEED studs. If you drive slow and wisely, you may not. But that's not what my point was.

The feds, under the Commerce Clause and the Property Clause of the US Constitution, retain exclusive federal authority over the water of navigable rivers: read ANILCA  at 43 US Code Sec. 3207.  The Submerged Lands Act transferred to the State only the title to the beds of navigable waterways, and ownership of the resources in the waters -- not title to or control over the waters themselves. The outside of the heated column cools, so water vapour condenses, forming a slightly conical cloud.  Inside that cloud wall, the rest of the heated column is still rising.  It is basically a pump lifting water from sea level to the top of the troposphere.
.
As with any vapour cycle engine, evaporation is fastest at the highest temp., and condensation is fastest at the coldest temp.  The bigger the temperature difference, the faster the pump works.
.
Air at 40C can hold more than twice as much water as air at 25C.  Water at 40C is more than twice as ready to evaporate as at 25C.
At the top, the condensed water is thrown out radially.
.
If the input water temperature and sea-level air temperature are high, and the bottom-to-top temp. difference is big, the pump works really hard.  The harder it pumps, the lower the pressure at the bottom, which sucks in more moister air, faster.
.
Irma was a big pump:
near record low pressure at sea level,
near record low temperature at high altitude.

Alceste: Public schools are in fact not religious institutions and some will reasonably object to religious rites of any sort being conducted in these buildings. I attended separate (Catholic) schools decades ago and as time went on religious observance was increasingly confined to actual churches. Where once mass on "holy days" was celebrated in the school, we were eventually expected to attend mass on holy days like Ash Wednesday and the Epiphany (when it fell on a weekday), on our own time and at church. When I was very young, we were given time off school for "Catholic holidays" but this was phased out as the separate school schedule and curriculum were aligned with Ontario Ministry of Education requirements. Few Catholics, except perhaps the clergy, objected. In the context of Western culture, religious freedom is for very valid historical reasons held to be synonymous with separation of church and state. To me, this is the basis of social peace and progress.

The Blood Bank supplies almost every hospital, base & clinic in Alaska.  To fulfill its mission it collects sufficient blood to cover any reasonable contingency.  Blood use is difficult to predict and blood products have strict use-by dates.  As a result, there will always be a number of units in the system that end up close to expiration.

To prevent this blood being wasted, the Blood Bank allows Alaskan hospitals & clinics to swap late-dated blood for fresh blood and takes it upon itself to place that blood at clinics that need it now.  To facilitate this, it has always had a flexible contract of one sort or another with an organization that will place a number of late units for it & will reimburse the Blood Bank for the cost of collection and shipping the blood.

This article omits the fact that fees are not paid directly to the advisor but rather to the advisor's firm.  Nor does it address the cost of running an advisory business.  

In the case of bank owned firms the house takes 50% or more of the fees charged.  Independent firms (non-bank) take a smaller portion of the fees, on the order of 20 - 40%.  

Bank owned firms take a larger percentage of the fees because they typically provide the advisor with an office, supplies and equipment including desk, phone, photocopier, etc., and support staff.  In the case of independent firms the advisor is left to cover the cost of these items themselves.

It shouldn't come as a surprise to anyone that a business has overhead to cover.  This is no different than getting your oil changed.  $300 at the dealership, $49 at "Quickie Change", or free (plus the cost of oil) if you do it yourself.  It's all a personal choice.  Just be sure you get value for what you pay for regardless of the service provided.

There were 31 people running for the three open seats, and while there were some great people, many were unqualified to hold public office. No amount of money from public coffers would have changed that, but it might have masked it. More importantly, though, it would be immoral to take $145,000 for a 10 week primary cycle when that is just slightly less than the cost of getting someone who is houseless off the streets and into affordable housing. For me, the choice is easy.
